transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2025-11-05 15:30 UTC
- Duration: ~48 minutes
- Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Sam (Redwood SE), Priya (Lumen Product), Mark (Lumen CTO), Jorge (Lumen Infra)

Summary (auto): Quick discovery on cost/unit economics; customer pre-qualified with a prototype running on open-source model, wants to understand cost run rates and migration path.

00:00 Alex (AE - Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick roll call?
00:08 Priya (Lumen): Priya here. Hi.
00:10 Mark (Lumen): Mark, hey.
00:12 Jorge (Lumen): Jorge.
00:14 Sam (SE - Redwood): Sam here. Thanks.
00:16 Alex: Cool. We're focused on unit econ — per token and the levers you can pull. Quick context from you, Priya, what's the product and target usage?
00:30 Priya: Sure. So we ship a conversational assistant embedded in our analytics product. Right now a small pilot — generating around 2k calls per day, but our roadmap targets 200k monthly active users in 9 months. The chat sessions tend to be long, like 400-800 tokens per session, and we expect a fair bit of re-use of system prompts.
00:55 Mark: The thing for us is budget predictability — we have a target of under $18k monthly for inference initially, and we want to know if that fits hosted or if we need reserved capacity.
01:10 Alex: Great. Quick question on latency SLOs? p95/p99 targets?
01:18 Jorge: p95 under 300ms ideally for assistant replies; p99 can be up to 700ms if necessary.
01:25 Sam: OK that's helpful — those latency targets push some real-time constraints, so that's where batching/caching tradeoffs matter.
01:35 Alex: I'll start with pricing primitives. Hosted is per-token consumption pricing, with optional request-level caching and automatic prefix/KV cache which reduces repeated prefix tokens. Dedicated is a committed GPU pool — you pay for reserved capacity but get much lower per-token run cost and predictable throughput. Private is more for full control and compliance.
01:58 Priya: Can you give an example? Like if we run 400 tokens per session and have 200k MAU, what's the math look like?
02:09 Sam: Sure, quick back-of-envelope. If you have 200k MAU with say 3 sessions per user per month, that's 600k sessions. At 400 tokens that's 240M tokens. On Hosted, with a hypothetical $0.00008 per token (encoder+decoder combined cynical example) that's about $19.2k/mo — so borderline. But with prefix caching, if your system prompt is 80 tokens and it's repeated across calls, you could save maybe 20% or more depending on reuse pattern.
02:50 Mark: That helps, but the hosted rate you quoted seems a tad higher than what we've seen. Anything for bulk discounts?
02:58 Alex: Yes. Hosted has tiered volume pricing and credits for predictable high-volume customers. Also, if you commit to Dedicated — e.g., reserved GPUs — the net per-token cost can drop substantially. For example, a mid-range dedicated pool might reduce our inference unit cost by 40-60% compared to list hosted. But you trade that for monthly commitment and you need to model utilization.
03:20 Priya: How do we think about batching? We worry about latency.
03:25 Sam: Batching helps amortize kernel and compute overhead across requests, lowering cost per token but adding queuing latency. Redwood's runtime has continuous batching that respects latency SLOs — you can set batching windows and max batch sizes. For your p95 target, we could keep batching small and rely more on KV/prefix caching to save costs without impacting p95. For bulk async workloads, you'd increase batching aggressively.
03:50 Jorge: Can we configure hybrid routing — like hosted for spikes and dedicated for steady traffic?
03:55 Alex: Absolutely. Smart routing can send requests to Dedicated while bursting to Hosted or another region — you can set cost/latency policies.
04:05 Mark: Security: We need SOC2 and customer data residency inside EU for EEA customers. Is that okay with hosted?
04:14 Alex: Hosted has region options and SOC2 compliance docs we can share. For strict EU residency + bring-your-own-key (BYOK), we recommend Dedicated or Private. But hosted still supports regional endpoints and KMS integrations for some enterprise tiers. We'll send you the SOC2 report and the KMS whitepaper.
04:35 Priya: Cool. Can you walk through a sample pricing slab for low, medium, high usage?
04:40 Sam: Sure — I can sketch 3 profiles quickly: 1) Early pilot: 10k sessions/mo, low batching, hosted, cost X — 2) Growth: 600k sessions/mo, mixed caching, hosted with volume discounts, cost Y — 3) Scale: committed Dedicated with 2-3 reserved GPUs, aggressive batching & quantization, cost Z. I'll attach a spreadsheet after the call.
05:05 Priya: What's 'quantization' do to quality? We're sensitive to hallucinations on financial language.
05:12 Sam: Good callout. Lower-bit quantization can increase inference throughput but may degrade quality depending on the model — Redwood supports multiple quantization profiles and we run noise/regression evals tied to your prompt set before recommending an aggressive profile. For finance-y prompts, we'd be conservative; maybe int8 with eval gate.
05:35 Mark: If we start hosted and later go Dedicated, how hard is migration?
05:40 Alex: It's designed to be low friction — same API surface, model pinning, and rollout policies. You can do a canary to Dedicated for a small percentage of traffic. Usually a few configuration changes and traffic routing.
05:54 Jorge: About caching — what is KV cache vs prefix cache? We heard both but not sure how they differ in practice.
06:00 Sam: Prefix cache stores the output tokens for repeated prompt prefixes — e.g., same system prompt; KV cache is the transformer key/value cache that keeps state for a session across turns enabling faster generation for multi-turn chat. Prefix cache helps when you have many identical starting prompts across users; KV cache helps minimize recomputation inside a single long session. Both reduce cost but in different patterns.
06:30 Priya: Any rough numbers on savings?
06:34 Sam: Hard to generalize — prefix caching with heavy reuse can cut repeated tokens by 20-60% depending on your reuse; KV cache saves compute on subsequent tokens in a session, often 10-40% depending on average turn length. We'll need sample logs to model precisely.
06:50 Mark: Our infra team worried about burst spikes causing failed requests if Dedicated is at capacity. What happens then?
06:57 Alex: There are fallback policies — you can route overload traffic to Hosted, or to a cheaper model variant with graceful degradation. Redwood also supports autoscaling and overprovisioning policies for Dedicated.
07:10 Jorge: On the Dedicated cost model — is licensing per-GPU or per-node? What are the commits?
07:16 Alex: It's a reserved capacity contract; pricing is expressed as monthly cost per reserved GPU-equivalent. Commit granularity depends on region and hardware. We provide CPU+GPU combos and can size based on your throughput profile. We'll include examples in the spreadsheet.
07:35 Priya: Could you show a concrete worked example for our projected 240M tokens/mo?
07:40 Sam: Roughly — hosted list at our earlier hypothetical rate would be ~19k; with typical volume discounts and prefix caching that could drop to 12-15k. Dedicated at 60-70% reduced per-token could be in the 6-8k equivalent run rate but you must cover monthly reservation costs, so you need >60% utilization to realize that benefit. If your utilization is lower, it's not worth it.
08:10 Mark: So the break-even utilization point is important. We'll need the formulas.
08:14 Alex: We'll provide break-even math in the spreadsheet — show per-token hosted vs amortized dedicated (reservation + ops) by utilization.
08:22 Priya: What's the expected latency delta between hosted and dedicated — all else equal?
08:27 Sam: Dedicated can often hit lower median latency because it avoids multi-tenant scheduling jitter, but hosted can be tuned with instance types. For your p95 300ms target, both can be configured; Dedicated gives more headroom at scale.
08:45 Jorge: Do you support bring-your-own-models on Dedicated/Private? We have an internal finetuned family of models.
08:50 Alex: Yes. Dedicated and Private allow you to run your own model images. Hosted can host certified open models from our catalog; private allows air-gapped deployments but needs more ops.
09:05 Mark: Any special contract terms around data retention and logs? We need limited retention and filtered logs for regulatory reasons.
09:12 Alex: Yes — retention and log redaction policies are configurable for Dedicated/Private; hosted has enterprise tiers for retention settings. We'll surface the exact SLAs and retention controls in the security packet.
09:25 Priya: Great. Final question: what's the typical onboarding timeline for pilot to production?
09:30 Alex: Pilot on Hosted can be done in days (some self-serve); Dedicated onboarding typically 4-8 weeks depending on procurement and capacity scheduling; Private (on-prem) can be several months.
09:45 Mark: Good enough. Let's wrap with next steps.
09:48 Alex: Recap: We'll send: 1) pricing slab w/ three profiles, 2) SOC2 + KMS notes, 3) Sam's preliminary cost simulation and batching notes. Jorge will share infra estimates. Any other asks?
09:58 Priya: Can you include an example of how quantization affected regression for a finance prompt?
10:03 Sam: Yep — we'll include a short eval note and thresholds.
10:08 Alex: Perfect. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up via email and Slack.
10:12 Meeting ends.
